questions.q: What are the three categories of target behind submitting a job in Azure Quantum?
options: Simulators, the resource estimator, and real third-party hardware (QPUs)
Development, staging, and production environments
Free tier, paid tier, and enterprise tier
Python, Q#, and openQASM
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes simulators (exact classical computation), the resource estimator (a cost/feasibility projection, not an execution), and real hardware (actual physical QPUs from third-party providers).

questions.q: Why is a wrong answer from a simulator run unambiguously a bug in your code, while a wrong answer from real hardware is not?
options: Simulators compute the exact mathematical result (up to floating-point precision) with no physical noise, so a wrong simulator result can only come from incorrect logic, whereas real hardware introduces genuine physical noise that can also produce a wrong-looking result
Simulators are always slower, which is the only difference
Real hardware always gives the mathematically perfect answer, unlike simulators
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: A simulator has no hardware noise -- it computes the exact result, so any wrong output is a logic bug. Real hardware can produce a wrong-looking result purely from physical noise, making bugs and noise hard to tell apart.

questions.q: What does the Azure Quantum resource estimator actually do with your program?
options: It executes the program and returns the measurement results, just more slowly than a simulator
It analyzes the compiled program and projects the physical qubits/runtime it would need on future fault-tolerant hardware, without executing it to get a result
It automatically rewrites your Q# code to use fewer qubits
It submits the program directly to a random real hardware provider
questions.explain: The resource estimator is explicitly not a simulator -- it doesn't run the program for a result, it projects what running it would cost in physical resources on hardware that doesn't exist yet.

questions.q: Why is Azure Quantum described as a 'marketplace model' rather than a single Microsoft-built quantum computer?
options: Microsoft supplies the workspace, tooling, and billing/submission layer, while separate third-party hardware partners supply the actual physical QPUs as providers, each with their own technology, pricing, and queue
Because users can resell their own quantum computers through the platform
Because 'marketplace' is purely a marketing term with no technical meaning here
Because every provider uses identical, interchangeable hardware
questions.explain: Azure Quantum's role is the dev tools, job submission, and billing layer; the physical QPUs come from distinct third-party hardware partners plugged in as providers, each with their own underlying technology.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the realistic order in which a project should move through simulator, resource estimator, and real hardware?
options: Real hardware first to see genuine results, then simulator, then resource estimator
Simulator first to validate correctness, then resource estimator to assess feasibility, then real hardware only with a specific reason to see behavior under real noise
Resource estimator first, since it's free, regardless of whether the algorithm is even correct yet
All three should always be run simultaneously on first attempt
questions.explain: The lesson recommends simulator first for cheap exact debugging, resource estimator once correctness is established to check hardware feasibility, and real hardware only once there's a specific reason to observe real noisy behavior -- not as a first debugging step.
